body_html:
Spanish word order is more flexible than English, but that flexibility hides a few firm rules that learners break all the time. Adjectives usually go after the noun, object pronouns usually go before the verb, and questions often swap the subject and verb. Get these right and your Spanish will instantly sound less translated. Here are the rules that matter most, with the mistakes I see learners make again and again.

Key takeaways
  • Most adjectives go after the noun: un carro rojo.
  • Some adjectives change meaning before the noun: un gran hombre vs un hombre grande.
  • Object pronouns go before a conjugated verb, or attach to infinitives, gerunds and positive commands.
  • Indirect before direct: te lo doy, and le lo becomes se lo.
{{toc}}

Spanish word order: the basic sentence

Like English, the default order is subject, verb, object: María compra pan (María buys bread). But Spanish verbs show who the subject is, so the subject is often dropped (Compro pan) or moved for emphasis (Pan compro yo, no tú). The RAE’s Nueva gramática describes this order as flexible and shaped by what the speaker wants to highlight.

Where adjectives go

Descriptive adjectives normally follow the noun:

  • una casa grande a big house
  • el vino tinto red wine
  • una película interesante an interesting movie

Numbers, quantities and possessives go before: dos perros, mucha gente, mi casa. Saying una roja casa is one of the most obvious signs of English interference.

Adjectives that change meaning

Before the nounAfter the noun
un gran hombre a great manun hombre grande a big man
un viejo amigo an old (long-time) friendun amigo viejo an elderly friend
pobre chico poor (unfortunate) boyun chico pobre a poor (not rich) boy
un nuevo carro a new (different) carun carro nuevo a brand-new car
la misma persona the same personla persona misma the person herself

Before the noun, adjectives often sound more subjective or poetic: una hermosa mañana is common in writing.

{{image:2}}

Object pronouns: before or after?

Before a conjugated verb

Lo veo. (I see it.) / Te llamo mañana. (I’ll call you tomorrow.) / No la conozco. (I don’t know her.)

Attached to infinitives, gerunds and positive commands

Quiero verlo. / Estoy leyéndolo. / ¡Dímelo! With an infinitive or gerund you can also put the pronoun before the first verb: Lo quiero ver, Lo estoy leyendo. Both are correct.

Negative commands: before

No lo hagas. (Don’t do it.) Never No hazlo.

Two pronouns: indirect first

Me lo dijo. (He told it to me.) / Te la presto. (I’ll lend it to you.) When le or les meets lo, la, los, las, it becomes se: Se lo di a María, never Le lo di.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Questions

In questions with a question word, the verb usually comes before the subject: ¿Qué quiere Juan? (What does Juan want?), ¿Dónde vive tu hermana? Spanish has no “do” helper, so ¿Qué Juan quiere? sounds wrong in most varieties. In the Caribbean you will hear ¿Qué tú quieres? with the pronoun before the verb; that is a regional feature, not a mistake. Yes/no questions can keep normal order and rely on intonation: ¿Tu hermana vive aquí?

Negatives

No goes before the verb and before any object pronouns: No lo sé (not Lo no sé). Spanish also uses double negatives: No veo nada, No viene nadie. If the negative word comes first, drop no: Nadie viene.

Word order for emphasis

Spanish moves things to the front to highlight them:

  • A mí me gusta el café. I (as for me) like coffee.
  • Ese libro ya lo leí. That book, I’ve already read it.
  • Llegó el verano. Summer has arrived (verb first for events).

The a mí me gusta structure is explained fully in {{link:how-to-use-gustar|how to use gustar}}.

Try it yourself

  1. She has a black cat. (Tiene un gato negro.)
  2. Tell me! (¡Dímelo!)
  3. I gave it to him. (Se lo di.)
  4. Where does your brother work? (¿Dónde trabaja tu hermano?)
  5. Don’t buy it. (No lo compres.)

Word order is one of several areas where literal translation leads you astray; see {{link:literal-translation-mistakes-spanish|literal translation mistakes}} and {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|my guide to common Spanish mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Spanish word order is forgiving, but a few rules are firm: adjectives after nouns, pronouns before conjugated verbs, se lo instead of le lo and verb before subject in questions. Master those and the rest is style.

faq.q: Do adjectives go before or after the noun in Spanish?
faq.a: Most descriptive adjectives go after the noun: una casa blanca. Numbers, quantities and possessives go before, and some adjectives like grande, viejo and pobre change meaning depending on position.

faq.q: Where do object pronouns go in Spanish?
faq.a: Before a conjugated verb (lo veo), attached to infinitives, gerunds and positive commands (verlo, viéndolo, dímelo) and before negative commands (no lo hagas).

faq.q: Why is it se lo and not le lo?
faq.a: When le or les comes before lo, la, los or las, Spanish changes it to se: Se lo di a María.
